name: Flocking

origin.note: Coordination without communication: the flocking problem.

summary: Robots must move together as a group, following a leader while roughly keeping a formation.
statement: Robots follow a designated leader whose path is not known in advance, while keeping (approximately) a given formation and avoiding collisions.

primer.intro: Think of a flock of birds following a leader whose route nobody knows in advance, keeping roughly the same shape and never bumping into each other. In the flocking problem, robots in the plane must follow a designated leader robot along an unpredictable path while keeping approximately a given formation (for example, a V shape) and avoiding collisions. The robots are oblivious (they forget everything after each move) and silent: they coordinate only by looking at each other's positions. The catalogue records only the first formal treatment [Gervasi2004Flocking] and has not checked its exact assumptions, so this page describes the problem and the simplest reasoning about it.

ideas.title: Keep your slot relative to the leader
ideas.idea:
A standard approach, assuming the followers can recognise the leader and know the target formation:
1. Look at all robots and find the leader.
2. Place the target formation with the leader at its tip, oriented, say, along the leader's last observed direction of motion.
3. Choose the free slot of the formation that is closest to you (with a fixed tie-break rule).
4. Move towards that slot, but never closer to another robot than a safety distance.
ideas.analysis: Each follower chases a target that moves with the leader, so if followers are fast enough they stay within a bounded distance of their slots. The details that make this hard are exactly those the model hides: an oblivious follower cannot remember the leader's past direction, and slot assignment must not change from look to look. We do not attribute this sketch to [Gervasi2004Flocking], whose method we have not read.
ideas.why_it_matters: Reducing a moving formation to "chase your slot" is the basic design idea of leader-follower formation control.

ideas.title: Followers must be faster than the leader
ideas.idea: Suppose followers can move no faster than the leader. Let the leader run at full speed in a straight line. A follower that is a distance $\delta > 0$ behind its slot moves at most as fast as the slot moves, so the gap never shrinks.
ideas.analysis: So exact formation keeping is impossible in general with equal top speeds; a follower can only stay within the error it started with. This simple observation, our own and not taken from a paper, is why flocking asks for approximate formations or gives followers extra speed.
ideas.why_it_matters: It explains why "approximately" in the problem statement is not a detail but a necessity.

history: Flocking was posed as a **coordination problem without communication** for oblivious robots [Gervasi2004Flocking]; the questions were feasibility and, later, fault tolerance and self-stabilisation.

measures.name: Time
measures.description: rounds (FSYNC, SSYNC) or epochs (ASYNC) until the task is done; "finite" when only solvability is known

measures.name: Colours
measures.description: colours of the light per robot (0 for oblivious robots)

variants.title: Oblivious robots following a leader
variants.summary: The first formal treatment of flocking by oblivious robots that communicate only by observing each other.

results.note: Introductory; the exact assumptions and guarantees were not read in the paper.

variants.notes: Self-stabilising and crash-tolerant flocking followed (SSS 2007, OPODIS 2008; not yet in the bibliography).

figure.caption: Flocking: the robots follow a leader (L) whose path is not known in advance, keeping approximately a given formation and avoiding collisions [Gervasi2004Flocking]. The animation shows the basic slot-chasing idea (not the method of [Gervasi2004Flocking]): in each round the leader moves; each follower places the V formation behind the leader's last observed heading, takes the nearest free slot (dashed circles) and moves towards it at a speed higher than the leader's.

frames.label: Start: followers scattered behind the leader L
Each round: L moves; followers chase their V slots
Final: L stops; the followers hold the V
